scope.source_catalog: english-forms.md, five actual tables A–E, 364 rows

indexes.name: Academy of American Poets · Glossary of Poetic Terms
indexes.boundaries: Every displayed index entry from Abecedarian through Zuihitsu, including unlinked entries. The index mixes forms, devices, meters, movements, roles and genres.

indexes.name: Poetry at Harvard · Glossary of Poetic Genres
indexes.boundaries: Every main glossary heading from allegory through verse epistle. Related words mentioned in descriptions were not counted as headings.

scope.coverage_limit: 198 index occurrences before cross-index deduplication; neither page is a census of English song and verse forms. Individual linked entries served as evidence rather than a recursively expanded discovery index.
scope.matching: Checked normalized and original names, aliases, catalog definitions and source-described differences. Nearest examples are comparisons only; a comparison does not assert historical descent or equivalence.
scope.classification: Two independent questions govern the comparison: whether an identifiable English genre or practice has a catalog identity, and whether the evidence supplies an enforceable structural rule. An absent genre may be a catalog-coverage gap even when it supplies no fixed stanza or meter. In the two bounded indexes, List Poem and Verbless Poetry are missing in specific organizational or constraint senses; two is not a total for missing genres, rhetorical forms, or traditions. Related examples in existing rows do not count as equivalence.
scope.english_use_rule: An original English work, a translation independently issued or presented as a work of poetry in English, or an authorized English performance or liturgical text attests use in English. An isolated English gloss or an explanation of a foreign-language form does not suffice. English reading use, actual English-language performance, English-original composition, and fidelity to a source-language metrical rule are independent claims; only the documented claim travels with an item.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Verbless Poetry

Verbless Poetry.definition: All the words in the poem avoid the verb category.
Verbless Poetry.attestation: The Academy identifies Ezra Pound’s In a Station of the Metro as an English example.
Verbless Poetry.catalog_distinction: Lipogram excludes written letters; it never excludes a part of speech. Applying the new constraint would require a convention for ambiguous participles.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · List Poem

List Poem.definition: An inventory, ordered or developed to make the poem, can supply its entire form.
List Poem.attestation: Christopher Smart’s cat passage in Jubilate Agno is an example on the Academy page.
List Poem.catalog_distinction: List song ties its catalogue to a recurring sung title or refrain. Neither a refrain nor a melody is inherent to catalog verse.

Blazon.definition: A descriptive inventory addresses a beloved feature by feature, frequently through comparisons.
Blazon.attestation: The Academy cites an English passage in Spenser’s Epithalamium. A blazon can occupy part of a larger work.
Blazon.catalog_distinction: The subject-specific enumeration goes beyond generic listing; the evidence does not require musical sections, a fixed body-part order or a sonnet.
Blazon.catalog_identity: No dedicated form row in the reviewed catalog
Blazon.structural_scope: feature-by-feature descriptive inventory; no fixed stanza, meter or one complete diagram established

Aubade.definition: A dawn lyric or song, often framing the end of a night together and impending separation.
Aubade.attestation: The Academy cites Donne’s The Sun Rising as an English example that resists the expected parting.
Aubade.catalog_distinction: Elegy can express loss but does not supply the dawn address. The tradition does not dictate stanza count or require a separation.
Aubade.catalog_identity: No dedicated form row in the reviewed catalog
Aubade.structural_scope: dawn lyric; occasion or address; no fixed stanza, meter or one complete diagram established

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Ars Poetica

Ars Poetica.definition: A poem centers on the art or practice of writing poetry.
Ars Poetica.attestation: The Academy identifies Pope’s An Essay on Criticism as an English instance.
Ars Poetica.catalog_distinction: The subject can occur in an epistle or other forms; the epistle’s letter structure is optional.

Ekphrasis.definition: A poem describes, interprets or otherwise responds to visual art.
Ekphrasis.attestation: The Academy cites Keats’s Ode on a Grecian Urn and Sasha Pimentel’s The Kiss.
Ekphrasis.catalog_distinction: An emblem joins an image, motto and verse. An ekphrastic work can refer to an artwork without reproducing it.

Fragment.definition: A deliberately partial or discontinuous poem can make its incompleteness part of the composition.
Fragment.attestation: The Academy names Coleridge’s Kubla Khan and earlier Romantic fragment titles.
Fragment.catalog_distinction: A zuihitsu can include fragments but does not subsume deliberate fragment poetry. Accidental textual loss is a different use of the word.

Fable.definition: Short narrative, often with personified agents, which carries a lesson. Only verse realizations are pertinent here.
Fable.attestation: The Academy names Emerson’s Fable and Bodenheim’s Rattlesnake Mountain Fable II.
Fable.catalog_distinction: Cante fable mixes spoken prose and sung insertions; an English verse fable can consist entirely of verse.
Fable.catalog_identity: No dedicated form row in the reviewed catalog
Fable.structural_scope: verse narrative carrying a lesson; no fixed stanza, meter or one complete diagram established

sources.title: Collection of translated metrical couplets · publisher announcement
Published book review · independent description of the English translations

Doha.definition: A self-contained South Asian couplet with asymmetrically divided lines.
Doha.attestation: A published volume presents more than half of a historical corpus in English couplets. Its translator uses meter and rhyme. The evidence does not establish that the English lines systematically preserve the original quantitative subdivisions.
Doha.catalog_distinction: A generic couplet does not encode the divisions. The summary and detailed wording differ about where the count applies; verify the traditional weight unit and English convention before encoding.
Doha.english_use: Published or presented for reading as poetry in English translation; English-original composition and performance in English were not established by these sources.

sources.title: Published English translation of a recorded oríkì · African Poems

Oríkì.definition: Yorùbá oral praise poetry strings together identifying praise names or epithets.
Oríkì.attestation: A poetry edition identifies the recorded Yorùbá praises, publishes a complete English translation as a poem, and describes the original sung practice. The translation attests use as English reading text; the recording does not attest an English performance.
Oríkì.catalog_distinction: The catalog’s canticle is a sacred text; it cannot substitute for this distinct, culturally situated tradition of naming.
Oríkì.english_use: Published or presented for reading as poetry in English translation; English-original composition and performance in English were not established by these sources.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Bhakti Poetry
Translated Hindi devotional lyrics · Murty Classical Library

Bhakti Poetry.definition: A family of South Asian devotional traditions, with diverse languages and practices.
Bhakti Poetry.attestation: A scholarly edition presents English translations of devotional lyrics as poetry, with a sample of the translated text. This establishes reading use for part of the tradition. A single shared English metrical form is not established.
Bhakti Poetry.catalog_distinction: A metrical hymn has its own stanza and tune conventions. Shared devotion cannot establish a shared form.
Bhakti Poetry.english_use: Published or presented for reading as poetry in English translation; English-original composition and performance in English were not established by these sources.

Nocturne.definition: A lyric organized around night or a night scene.
Nocturne.attestation: The Academy identifies Donne’s A Nocturnal upon S. Lucy’s Day as an English example.
Nocturne.catalog_distinction: An elegy can also be a nocturne, but mourning imposes no nighttime setting and night imposes no stanza shape.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Praise Poem

Praise Poem.definition: Verse praising or thanking a subject.
Praise Poem.attestation: The Academy cites W. S. Merwin’s Thanks alongside Elizabeth Alexander’s Praise Song for the Day.
Praise Poem.catalog_distinction: A praise chorus repeats a sung refrain; a praise poem need not be sung, sacred or repetitive.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Inaugural Poem

Inaugural Poem.definition: A poem written or delivered for an inauguration.
Inaugural Poem.attestation: The Academy has a dedicated English-language presidential-inauguration entry.
Inaugural Poem.catalog_distinction: Public occasion supplies the classification. Direct address can feature, but no letter or stanza form is entailed.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Occasional Poem

Occasional Poem.definition: Verse responding to a specific occasion or event.
Occasional Poem.attestation: Both indexes recognize this public or personal occasion category.
Occasional Poem.catalog_distinction: Greeting-card verse serves some occasions but adds a short patterned delivery; the umbrella allows many structures.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Nonsense verse

Nonsense verse.definition: Whimsical verse works through sound, invented language or semantic incongruity.
Nonsense verse.attestation: The Academy features Lear and Carroll’s Jabberwocky.
Nonsense verse.catalog_distinction: A nonsense refrain is narrower than an entire nonsense poem. Limerick and Nursery rhyme already cover some examples.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Chance Operations

Chance Operations.attestation: The Academy documents chance procedures in its dedicated entry.
Chance Operations.catalog_distinction: A cut-up physically divides and reorders source text, which can be done deliberately. A chance operation need not use cut text.

Madrigal.definition: The term covers several musical and verse traditions, including an early Italian tercet-and-couplet practice.
Madrigal.attestation: The Academy distinguishes Italian prototypes and later freer English madrigals, and supplies an Elizabethan English text.
Madrigal.catalog_distinction: Row 143 describes the English sung setting. The added historical text pattern must not be imposed on every English madrigal.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Blues Poem

Blues Poem.definition: Blues poetry draws on an oral and musical tradition. One common stanza states a line, varies or repeats it, then answers it.
Blues Poem.attestation: The linked glossary explicitly says that the three-line pattern is optional in blues poetry.
Blues Poem.catalog_distinction: An AAB lyric stanza can coincide with the twelve-bar musical cycle in row 35. A written poem establishes no bar count, and blues poems can take other stanza shapes. Stanza labels may lead to row 35 as related search terms without asserting equivalence.

Epithalamion.definition: A song or poem for a wedding.
Epithalamion.attestation: Harvard lists the genre. The Academy’s Blazon entry quotes Spenser’s English Epithalamium.
Epithalamion.catalog_distinction: A wedding song has a specific occasion with no requirement for a greeting card’s rhyme or quatrain count.
Epithalamion.catalog_identity: No dedicated form row in the reviewed catalog
Epithalamion.structural_scope: wedding lyric; occasion; no fixed stanza, meter or one complete diagram established

Palinode.definition: A poem retracts or revises an earlier assertion, often in dialogue with an earlier poem.
Palinode.attestation: Harvard defines the term. The Poetry Foundation publishes Sasha Steensen’s English poem Palinode.
Palinode.catalog_distinction: A letter can recant, but a palinode can take other shapes. Its relation to the earlier statement is constitutive.
Palinode.catalog_identity: No dedicated form row in the reviewed catalog
Palinode.structural_scope: recantation or revision of an earlier statement; no fixed stanza, meter or one complete diagram established

Georgic.definition: Verse centered on agricultural work, land management or husbandry.
Georgic.attestation: Harvard lists the georgic alongside pastoral traditions.
Georgic.catalog_distinction: A pastoral singing dialogue and georgic agricultural labor are distinct conventions. Neither supplies a fixed georgic stanza.

Paean.definition: A song of triumph or joyful acclaim.
Paean.attestation: Harvard lists the paean as a song genre.
Paean.catalog_distinction: An extant praise chorus may serve a different religious purpose; a paean need not cycle a chorus.

Panegyric.definition: An encomium in poem or song praising a particular subject.
Panegyric.attestation: Harvard lists it. The Academy’s Praise Poem entry describes a related broader category.
Panegyric.catalog_distinction: Its praising function is more relevant than any sectional pattern. Review alongside Praise Poem to avoid manufacturing a duplicate form.

Romance.definition: A medieval or chivalric adventure tale can be written in verse.
Romance.attestation: Harvard identifies medieval verse romances and the Spanish ballad tradition.
Romance.catalog_distinction: Narrative story song gives a sung story shape. Adventure, historical genre and manner of narration do not mandate that shape.

Light verse.definition: A broad category of playful or comic verse.
Light verse.attestation: Harvard explicitly describes a range extending across nonsense and song.
Light verse.catalog_distinction: Clerihew, Limerick and Double dactyl are represented shapes within its range.

Invective.definition: A sustained denunciation or verbal attack.
Invective.attestation: Harvard lists invective, specifying abusive personal denunciation.
Invective.catalog_distinction: Flyting requires an exchange between opponents; invective may be only one voice.

Parody.definition: Comic imitation of an identifiable model.
Parody.attestation: Harvard lists parody as a genre.
Parody.catalog_distinction: A contrafactum fits a new text to existing music; comic imitation can operate on diction, style or other features without reusing a tune. Their overlap depends on the work. The reviewed aliases do not equate them.

Satire.definition: Ridicule that directs attention toward a perceived fault.
Satire.attestation: Harvard lists satire as a genre.
Satire.catalog_distinction: An epigram can be satirical, but satire can organize a long work in many verse forms.

Tragedy.definition: A dramatic genre traditionally associated with a protagonist’s downfall.
Tragedy.attestation: Harvard tracks its origins in Greek verse drama.
Tragedy.catalog_distinction: Verse drama already supplies acts, scenes and voices. Tragedy distinguishes the dramatic action rather than prescribing a new verse layout.

Pastoral.definition: Poetry concerned with the rural world and its representation.
Pastoral.attestation: Both glossaries identify an extended pastoral tradition.
Pastoral.catalog_distinction: The Eclogue row describes a pastoral dialogue. No reviewed alias independently establishes a pastoral-elegy row, and a pastoral poem need not be a dialogue or an elegy.

Allegory.definition: Narrative conveys a second sustained level of meaning.
Allegory.attestation: Both indexes recognize allegory; Harvard explicitly includes it among genres.
Allegory.catalog_distinction: Emblems can be allegorical. A sustained allegory does not require a picture or motto and may take numerous forms.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Nature Poetry

Nature Poetry.definition: Poems engaging with nature or the environment.
Nature Poetry.attestation: The Academy indexes this thematic category.
Nature Poetry.catalog_distinction: Eclogues can discuss the environment but use additional pastoral conventions.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Political Poetry

Political Poetry.definition: Political content cuts across many formal designs.
Political Poetry.attestation: The Academy indexes political poetry. The catalog includes the specific Irish vision tradition.
Political Poetry.catalog_distinction: An aisling exemplifies only one tradition; political speech alone supplies no stanza formula.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Lyric Poetry

Lyric Poetry.definition: A wide historical category of often brief, voiced or musical poems.
Lyric Poetry.attestation: Both indexes describe lyric as a large category.
Lyric Poetry.catalog_distinction: Many cataloged forms can be lyric; the selected sonnet is an example, not a synonym.

sources.title: Academy of American Poets · Poetic Contest

Poetic Contest.attestation: The Academy indexes poetic contest and the catalog contains specific contest structures.
Poetic Contest.catalog_distinction: Tenson, Flyting and Battle rap establish different turn-taking conventions; the umbrella introduces no single new pattern.

Incantation.definition: Repeated utterance used to invoke or enact a ritual effect.
Incantation.attestation: The Academy identifies the ritual or magical function.
Incantation.catalog_distinction: The catalog’s metrical charm is an example; incantation alone does not require its directions or closing prayer.

Aphorism.definition: Compact formulation of an observation or maxim.
Aphorism.attestation: The Academy identifies its instructive function.
Aphorism.catalog_distinction: Gnomic verse already permits one- or two-line maxims. Aphorisms in prose do not establish another verse shape.

Proverb.definition: Short saying conveying a general truth.
Proverb.attestation: The Academy indexes proverb by its expressive function.
Proverb.catalog_distinction: The gnomic entry expressly covers poetic sequences of maxims. A proverb need not be verse.
